student_profile.student_background: Practicing healthcare professionals across roles — clinicians, nurses, allied health staff, administrators, and researchers — non-technical, no programming assumed. The audience spans the three levels of the organization's AI taxonomy, and a single course serves all three: Operators (limited end-user interaction with the AI; need to accurately interpret outputs and ensure the technology enhances rather than replaces judgement); Contributors (interact with the AI but do not make decisions about the technology); and Shapers (interact with the AI and hold decision-making capacity).
student_profile.aggregate_academic_performance: Experienced adult professionals with strong domain readiness; mixed comfort and confidence with AI tools.
student_profile.anticipated_learner_needs_and_barriers: Wide variation in AI fluency; assume little formal AI training. Learners engage best with REAL, concrete material — actual clinical risk scores, published studies, documented device cases — not abstract principles. Plain language, terms defined on first use, short daily sessions.

instructor_preferences.instructor_emphasis_intent: This module teaches the pros and cons of AI assistants in diagnosis and patient management through REAL, VERIFIABLE material. Named tools, published studies, real device cases, and validated clinical scores ARE allowed and encouraged — but every named fact, number, and example MUST come from the provided source excerpts; never invent or embellish an example, statistic, or citation. When citing a named study, score, tool, or report, include its source URL from the excerpts on the slide. Cover the benefits (pros) and the risks and limitations (cons) with equal seriousness, and give substantive treatment to safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability. Address what the Operator, the Contributor, and the Shaper each need to interpret, do, and decide.
instructor_preferences.instructor_style_preferences: Engagement-first case-based teaching, modeled on the client's own course style: open every session with a real hook (a published study, a documented device case, or a validated risk score from the sources); use patient-vignette slides in the format 'Patient facts, then AI says: ..., then Physician thinks: ..., then the reasoning takeaway'; include one discussion-cases slide per session with judgment scenarios that have no clean answer; use structured workflow tables (stage, is AI helpful?, example) where they teach better than prose; punchy short dialogues and light humor are welcome; slides stay dense (4-6 substantive bullets or a full table/vignette) and every named example carries its source URL.
instructor_preferences.instructor_focus_for_assessment: Assess judgment: scenario analysis, pros-and-cons reasoning, and when to trust, verify, or escalate an AI suggestion. No exams, no coding.

course_structure.course_learning_outcomes: Explain in plain language how AI assistants support diagnosis, clinical decisions, and patient management, using real documented examples; weigh the benefits against the risks and limitations, grounded in published evidence (validated risk scores, external-validation studies, real adverse-event reports); apply safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability to judge whether and how far to trust an AI output; keep clinical judgment central — AI supports, clinicians decide; and understand what the Operator, Contributor, and Shaper each must know and decide.
course_structure.weekly_schedule_outline: AI Assistants for Diagnosis and Patient Management: how AI supports diagnosis, clinical decisions, care planning, and patient monitoring — taught through real material from the provided sources: validated clinical risk scores (the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index) as the baseline for what 'validated' means; the published external validation of a widely deployed proprietary sepsis prediction model as the central cautionary tale about local performance, alert fatigue, and over-trust; real FDA MAUDE adverse-event reports for a surgical navigation system as the device-safety case study; the 2015 pigeon pathology study as a memorable hook about what image classification is and is not; and FDA guidance (Good Machine Learning Practice, Clinical Decision Support guidance, the AI/ML Action Plan) for what validation, transparency, and oversight require; covering the benefits — earlier detection, workload support, consistent monitoring — versus the risks — automation bias, false positives and negatives, opaque reasoning, alert fatigue, and degraded real-world performance; with safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability applied throughout, and the Operator, Contributor, and Shaper roles addressed in every session

assessment_design.assessment_format_preferences: No exams and no coding. Scenario Judgment (40%) — work real-material scenarios (an AI risk flag disagrees with clinical impression; an alert fires on a patient who looks fine) and justify trust, verification, and escalation decisions. Pros-and-Cons Analysis (35%) — for AI in diagnosis and patient management, argue both sides from the evidence. Discussion participation (25%) — engage the no-clean-answer cases.
assessment_design.assessment_delivery_constraints: Short applied deliverables submitted via the learning platform.

teaching_constraints.platform_policy_constraints: Institution-approved learning platform; accessibility standards; no patient-identifiable information. Named tools, studies, and device cases are permitted when drawn from the provided public sources with attribution.
teaching_constraints.ta_support_availability: Facilitator-led or self-paced; no teaching assistant assumed.
teaching_constraints.instructional_delivery_context: Professional development delivered as ~1-hour daily sessions; this demo module spans 5-6 such sessions built around real cases, vignettes, and discussion.

institutional_requirements.program_learning_outcomes: Aligns with the digital-education program's goals for responsible AI adoption and sound clinical judgment about AI.
institutional_requirements.academic_policies_and_institutional_stan: All named examples, statistics, and cases must be traceable to the provided public sources (attribution on slide); no fabricated content; no patient-identifiable information; clinical-ethics norms respected.
institutional_requirements.department_syllabus_requirements: Module must include learning outcomes, session structure, the assessment approach, and a sources page listing every cited source with its URL.

prior_feedback.historical_course_evaluation_results: Revision of an earlier draft. Client feedback on the previous version: too generic and not engaging — needs real named examples (real risk calculators, published studies, documented device cases) with sources shown, patient vignettes, discussion cases, and workflow tables, in the style of the client's own course materials; one module only for this demo; every fact grounded in real sources with no false information.

session_structure: Divide this module into 5-6 one-hour sessions. A natural split: Session 1 — what AI assistants do across diagnosis and patient management, opened with the pigeon-study hook and anchored by the PESI example of what a validated score looks like; Session 2 — the risks: the sepsis-model external validation as the central case, automation bias, false positives/negatives, alert fatigue; Session 3 — safety and trustworthiness: the MAUDE device reports as the case study, when human review is required, AI supports / clinicians decide; Session 4 — validation and explainability: what GMLP and the FDA guidance require, why local validation matters, the black-box problem; Session 5 — the three roles: what the Operator, Contributor, and Shaper each do and decide, with patient vignettes and a decision-point scenario; Session 6 — synthesis: discussion cases, pros-and-cons exercise, and the sources page. Open each session with a divider slide titled exactly "Session N: <focus>" and close each with a short knowledge check.
engagement_style: Teach like the client's own decks: (1) OPEN each session with a real hook from the source excerpts — a published study, a documented device case, or a validated score — never with definitions. (2) Use PATIENT VIGNETTES in exactly this format on their own slides: patient facts as short bullets, then 'AI says:' with the AI's output in quotes, then 'Physician thinks:' with the clinical reasoning, then a one-line takeaway. (3) When a slide cites a named study, score, tool, or report, put its SOURCE URL from the excerpts at the bottom of the slide. (4) Include one DISCUSSION CASES slide per session: 3-5 numbered judgment scenarios with a one-line 'no clean answer' framing (e.g., 'Two AI systems disagree. What do you do?'). (5) Use structured TABLES for workflow-fit content: rows = stages, columns = 'AI helpful?' and 'Example'. (6) Short punchy dialogues and light humor are welcome (e.g., AI: 'No medication allergies.' Patient: 'Penicillin almost killed me.' Clinician: 'Good thing I asked.'). (7) NEVER invent a named example, number, or citation — if it is not in the excerpts, teach it generically or leave it out.
